G0 — Design guideline: doc 14 realised

Reference board, not a screen. Realises doc 14 §2 (theme substrate + token roles), §3 (the honesty-label vocabulary: verification badge, layer chip, overlay chips, both-sides dispute), §4 (the trace panel), and §7 (type scale, spacing, motion, accessibility, copy voice). It composes nothing from doc 13's screen inventory — this is the vocabulary the C0* and S* fragments reuse, never re-derive.

1 — Theme substrate: token palette (doc 14 §2)

Every colour below is a CSS custom property, never a literal hex — the same code-graph-theme.ts pattern doc 14 §2 requires: name a token role, let the role resolve through the theme. The two panels are the identical swatch set rendered once under .theme-light and once under .theme-dark, so a reviewer can compare values directly rather than toggling.

--foregroundprimary text
--cardboard surface

--destructiveconflict role
--warningcaution role
--successstate-chip: populated
--infostate-chip: loading
--chart-1trace arm: semantic
--chart-2trace arm: keyword
--chart-3trace arm: ppr
--chart-4reserved — never an arm
--chart-5trace arm: rerank / code mark
--ringfocus outline

neutral token: --muted / --muted-foreground used by: candidate badge, layer chips
supported token: --primary used by: corroborated (outline), confirmed (filled)
caution token: --warning (same computed value as the amber --chart-4 ramp member) used by: overlay chips, degraded banner, lifecycle amber
conflict token: --destructive used by: disputed badge, dispute panel, error state
Four status roles, no new palette (doc 14 §3.1). --chart-4 carries the same amber hue as --warning but is reserved for score-arm identity only (§4 below) — status caution copy always reads --warning, never --chart-4 directly, so an arm bar can never be misread as a caution signal.

2 — Type scale & spacing (doc 14 §2, §7)

Board / section title21px / 640 — headings keep their larger sizes
Board-title chrome15px / 640 — .board-title
Body copy — the floor14px / text-sm — darkraise-ui default, no text-xs anywhere
Annotation callout copy12.5px — .annotation
entity_name · commit_sha · L2var(--font-mono) — identifiers only (doc 14 §7)
Known gap, flagged rather than papered over. Doc 14 §2/§9 fixes text-sm (14px) as the floor for all app text including badges and chips — compactness must come from padding and weight, never sub-floor type, "because a label carrying the system's central truth claim must not be the smallest text on the screen." The shared mockup.css chrome committed in Task 1 currently sizes .badge (12.5px), .layer-chip / .overlay-* (11.5px) and .state-chip (11px) below that floor. This board renders those classes as given rather than overriding shared chrome from within a single fragment — noted here as a doc-14-vs-asset gap for a follow-up mockup.css pass, not silently resolved.
--radius0.5rem — board frame, buttons
--radius-mdradius − 2px
--radius-smradius − 4px — chips
Density (cozy), elevation (medium), and radius (rounded) are locked axes — pinned, no switcher UI (doc 14 §2). Doc 14 does not fix a numeric spacing scale beyond the built-ins' own defaults ("the mockup sub-phase places components on the grid the theme already fixes"); this board's own chrome is the concrete illustration in practice — page gap 32px, board padding 20px, board-body gap 14px, annotation indent 12px — not a separate doc-14-specified ramp.

3 — Motion & accessibility (doc 14 §7, §8)

Motion — a closed list of signal uses, nothing decorative
  • Live-feed row entrance (a new event arriving)
  • Pipeline stepper's phase advance
  • Badge rung-change transition — a single subtle emphasis pulse when a fact's rung changes under a live update (pulse-glow keyframe)
  • The existing particle/aurora backdrop, reserved for the unauthenticated threshold surfaces (login / setup)
Accessibility — part of the encoding, not a pass afterwards
  • Colour never carries meaning alone — every state pairs a token colour with an icon and a text label; fill style + border style + icon differ pairwise even with colour removed
  • Contrast of label text against its chip background meets WCAG AA at text-sm in both modes — checkable once per theme via the token mapping, not per screen
  • Badges are focusable; the expansion opens on focus as well as hover (Popover for the full origin list — a tooltip cannot hold interactive content)
  • Counts are always printed beside a bar or ramp cell, never shading alone (calendar heatmap, trace-panel arms)
  • All motion honours prefers-reduced-motion
Every non-motion, non-a11y note above is restated inline on the vocabulary examples below rather than collected separately — an annotation next to a treatment is what makes the rule checkable against the pixels, not a rule stated once and trusted to hold.

4 — Honesty visual vocabulary (doc 14 §3, §4)

4a — The verification badge: all four rungs
candidate expansion — "extracted signal, not yet corroborated — served labelled"
corroborated expansion — rendered verbatim from the wire, never re-assembled client-side (doc 12 badge.claim)
canonical reference string (doc 12 §4) — asserted by K distinct origins of kinds [X, Y], no known contradiction, as of T
human-ratified expansion — claim string + ", human-ratified" suffix + who/when, e.g. "asserted by 4 distinct origins of kinds [memory, code, human], no known contradiction, as of 2026-07-20, human-ratified — ratified by a.lee, 2026-07-21"
disputed expansion (two-sided form) — disputed: 2 origins assert X, 1 origin asserts not-X, as of T — see the split panel in 4d
corroborated code@a3f19c2 a code-originated corroborated fact also carries this distinct mark inside its expansion — {commit_sha, basis, file_path, symbol_key} (doc 14 §3.2; C01 formalises the full composition)
Visible label is the rung name, with confirmed shown as "human-ratified" — never the word "verified" anywhere in label, tooltip, or state copy (rule 2). Icons are semantic, never decorative: dashed circle is incompleteness, the merge glyph is multiple distinct origins converging, the person-check is "a human ratified this," the scales are two sides held in balance. A plain checkmark appears nowhere in the ladder.
Two badge non-rung treatments exist outside this ladder (C01 renders both in full): an L0 memory carries no verification badge at all — a lifecycle amber label instead — and a terminal superseded L3 article shows an amber superseded badge that replaces the rung. Neither is a fifth rung; the CHECK constraint stays exactly candidate | corroborated | disputed | confirmed.
4b — The layer chip
L0 · memory L2 · fact L3 · article
Surface-toned, monospace, no accent, no status colour — classification, not judgement (doc 14 §3.3). Always precedes the verification badge in a row's label cluster so the reading order is "what kind of thing → how well supported." L1 (the candidate graph) is never directly served, so no L1 chip renders on a served row (doc 12 §4) — it is omitted above rather than shown unused.
4c — Overlay chips: riding a rung, never becoming one
corroborated under-sourced expansion — "origin count dropped below N; will demote if not re-corroborated"
corroborated stale expansion — "synthesised before the latest verified change"
Overlays append after the badge and never replace, recolour, or restyle it — the row is still corroborated, claim string intact, while the demotion hysteresis runs (doc 14 §3.4, doc 08 §4.3). The dashed border is the shared "provisional/overlay" marker across the language — the same non-colour channel candidate uses.
4d — The both-sides dispute treatment
disputed: 2 origins assert X, 1 origin asserts not-X, as of T
disputed asserts X — cookie_secure defaults to enabled in production 2 origins · kinds [memory, code]
vs
disputed asserts not-X — cookie_secure is tri-state, unset by default 1 origin · kind [human]
Strictly equal visual weight both sides — same card treatment, same type, no comparative bar or "2 vs 1" scoreboard, because corroboration count does not adjudicate a dispute (doc 14 §3.5). Order is deterministic and epistemically neutral: the earlier-asserted side renders first, stable across reloads — never ordered by count or recency, since that would visually pick the winner the backend refuses to pick (doc 14 §9).
4e — The surfaced-exclusion strip
3 facts excluded by context conflict — active context chip env=prod by_context_conflict
2 rows excluded — outside the current project scope by_project
0 shown, 5 excluded — every candidate row was filtered by the active scope/context, never rendered as a bare empty
The strip sits between the query controls and the rows, persistent — not a toast — and the empty state is computed after it, so "0 shown, N excluded" can never render as "nothing found" (doc 14 §3.6, §5; invariant 14). Each chip expands to its reason and, where the cause is a user-held control, points at it.
4f — The trace-panel style
region 1 — request header query: "cookie_secure default" · sectioned (fused=false) · channels ran: [semantic, keyword] · weights: w_semantic=0.7, w_keyword=0.3, w_ppr=0
region 2 — exclusion strip (shared with 4e) 1 row excluded — by_status
region 3 — per-row label cluster
L2 · fact corroborated context: matched · provenance: LLM-guessed, not human-checked
region 4 — score breakdown (ledger, not narrative)
semantic0.78
keyword0.41
pprw=0 · inactive
rerank6.6 / 10
rrf_score is printed as the ordering signal, not a bar among the modality arms (doc 14 §4) — the per-modality score survives on the row but must not be misread as rank.
Field-for-field rendering of doc 07 §8's payload — ledger, not narrative; no generated "because" sentence (doc 14 §4, invariant 15). Arm bars use only the four non-caution chart members (--chart-1/2/3/5), never --chart-4, so a bar can never be misread as a caution signal. A w_* = 0 arm renders as an inactive, muted bar labelled "inactive" — never omitted (which would hide that the arm exists) and never a zero score (which would imply it ran and found nothing) — invariant 23.

C01 — Verification badge matrix

The most-reused honesty component. Realises doc 14 §3.1 (status colour roles), §3.2 (the verification-badge ladder), §3.3 (layer chip, used here only as context), and §3.4 (overlay chips). This is the exact .badge / .overlay-* / .badge-code markup that every other board rendering an L2 fact or L3 article (S05 supersession lineage, S06/S07 Knowledge, S09 articles, S11 review mode, the trace panel in S03) composes verbatim rather than re-deriving. One matrix board, all variants side by side, in both themes.

1 — The four ladder rungs

candidate served labelled, below the ladder's supported rungs — "extracted signal, not yet corroborated — served labelled"
corroborated asserted by 3 distinct origins of kinds [code, memory], no known contradiction, as of 2026-07-20
K (here 3) binds to COUNT(DISTINCT origin_key) from fact_sources — never a row count. Two agents re-saving the same claim, or one repo re-derived across many commits, are one origin, not two; when origin identity is unknown the count undercounts rather than manufacturing agreement.
disputed: 2 origins assert X, 1 origin asserts not-X, as of T
disputed asserts X — the reranker is enabled by default in production 2 origins · kinds [memory, code]
vs
disputed asserts not-X — the reranker is opt-in per profile, disabled by default 1 origin · kind [human]
human-ratified asserted by 4 distinct origins of kinds [memory, code, human], no known contradiction, as of 2026-07-20, human-ratified — ratified by q.tran, 2026-07-21
Visible chip text is the rung name; confirmed always renders as "human-ratified" — never the word "verified", and never "confirmed" as visible text — with the claim string carrying the trailing ", human-ratified" suffix. Disputed shows both sides at strictly equal weight, earlier-asserted side first, no comparative bar, no picked winner (doc 14 §3.5).

2 — Overlay chips: riding a still-corroborated row, never a fifth rung

corroborated under-sourced origin count dropped below N; will demote if not re-corroborated
corroborated stale synthesised before the latest verified change
Both overlays append after the badge and never recolour, restyle, or replace it — the row is still corroborated, claim string intact, while the demotion hysteresis runs. The CHECK constraint stays exactly candidate | corroborated | disputed | confirmed; under-sourced and stale are label overlays on that rung, never a fifth ladder value (doc 14 §3.4).

3 — The code@commit corroborated variant

corroborated code@a3f19c2 L2 · fact
asserted by 2 distinct origins of kinds [code, memory], no known contradiction, as of 2026-07-19 — code-originated, born corroborated: parse is verification
commit_sha
a3f19c2
basis
function signature — parsed from def search(query: str) -> SearchResult
file_path
backend/app/services/pipeline.py
symbol_key
ProcessingPipeline.process_batch
A code-originated fact whose origin_kinds include code shows this distinct code@commit mark inside the expansion; fact_get / dispute_inspect return the full {commit_sha, basis, file_path, symbol_key} provenance detail (doc 12 §4, doc 14 §3.2). The parse itself is the corroborating origin, so a code-derived fact can be born corroborated without waiting on a second, independent memory-derived origin.

no verification badge renders for this row at all — badge: null, verification_status: null on the wire; superseded_by is null here too (retained, not currently pointing at a successor).

The CHECK constraint stays exactly candidate | corroborated | disputed | confirmed either way — neither treatment is a fifth rung (doc 14 §3.2).

C02 — Layer chip reference: L0 · L2 · L3, and the L1 that never renders

Formalises doc 14 §3.3's layer chip as its own reusable reference. The layer chip is an orthogonal axis, styled orthogonally from the verification badge — surface-toned .layer-chip using only --card/--border tokens, monospace layer key, no accent, no status colour — so "L2" is never misread as a trust level. It always precedes the verification badge in a row's label cluster (doc 13 §4's layer row field: L0 / L2 / L3, L1 never directly served).
L0 · memory Used by: Memories search & detail, Chat context panel, the retrieval trace's per-row cluster, and the nested row under a fact it supports (see below). token role: surface-toned --muted / --muted-foreground, bordered with --border — no accent, no status colour (realises doc 14 §3.3's "surface-toned … like the technologies chips" intent; the chip must stay visible against the --card board, so --muted, not --card) expansion — "memory — Layer 0 of the vault"
L2 · fact Used by: Knowledge → Facts tab & detail, the Review tab (disputed / under-sourced facts), and search / retrieval trace rows. token role: surface-toned --muted / --muted-foreground, bordered with --border — no accent, no status colour (realises doc 14 §3.3's "surface-toned … like the technologies chips" intent; the chip must stay visible against the --card board, so --muted, not --card) expansion — "fact — Layer 2 of the vault"
L3 · article Used by: Knowledge → Articles tab & detail, and search / retrieval trace rows. token role: surface-toned --muted / --muted-foreground, bordered with --border — no accent, no status colour (realises doc 14 §3.3's "surface-toned … like the technologies chips" intent; the chip must stay visible against the --card board, so --muted, not --card) expansion — "article — Layer 3 of the vault"
L0 · memory Used by: Memories search & detail, Chat context panel, the retrieval trace's per-row cluster, and the nested row under a fact it supports (see below). token role: surface-toned --muted / --muted-foreground, bordered with --border — no accent, no status colour (realises doc 14 §3.3's "surface-toned … like the technologies chips" intent; the chip must stay visible against the --card board, so --muted, not --card) expansion — "memory — Layer 0 of the vault"
L2 · fact Used by: Knowledge → Facts tab & detail, the Review tab (disputed / under-sourced facts), and search / retrieval trace rows. token role: surface-toned --muted / --muted-foreground, bordered with --border — no accent, no status colour (realises doc 14 §3.3's "surface-toned … like the technologies chips" intent; the chip must stay visible against the --card board, so --muted, not --card) expansion — "fact — Layer 2 of the vault"
L3 · article Used by: Knowledge → Articles tab & detail, and search / retrieval trace rows. token role: surface-toned --muted / --muted-foreground, bordered with --border — no accent, no status colour (realises doc 14 §3.3's "surface-toned … like the technologies chips" intent; the chip must stay visible against the --card board, so --muted, not --card) expansion — "article — Layer 3 of the vault"
A layer chip classifies, never asserts standing (doc 14 §3.3): an L2 fact may still be a candidate on the verification ladder, or a disputed one — the layer says "what kind of thing," the badge says "how well supported," and the reading order in a label cluster is always layer chip first, badge second.
L1 · candidate graph Not a live chip variant — L1 is never directly served. The row-level layer field (doc 13 §4) only ever takes L0 / L2 / L3; there is no served row for a layer chip to label L1 with. L1 is the pre-corroboration extraction graph, and it is rendered elsewhere — as node/edge structure in the Memory Graph explorer — never as a labelled row in a result list or trace panel. no expansion string — there is nothing to classify a served row as, because no served row is ever L1
Rendered here as a dashed, ghosted placeholder deliberately unlike the three live chips above, so a reviewer sees what is absent from a row's label cluster rather than assuming L1 was forgotten.
L2 · fact cookie_secure defaults to Secure only when environment=production corroborated
L0 · memory "set COOKIE_SECURE=false for plain-HTTP LAN deploys" — memory, 2026-06-09 grouping.relation = "supports fact F"
The grouping-under-fact collapse (doc 13 §4, doc 07 §5): a memory that supports a fact renders nested under it, indented, rather than as a third unrelated hit beside it — so a memory, the fact it supports, and an article citing that fact never read as three unrelated rows. The relation string travels verbatim from grouping.relation; note the L0 memory row carries no badge (a memory's verification_status is always null — it has a lifecycle label instead, not a rung), while the L2 fact it supports carries the full ladder.

C03 — Global chrome: nav shell, scope controls, command palette

Reference board, not a screen. Realises doc 13 §3 (the three-group / eight-destination navigation map, the project switcher as global scope, the separate session context chip) and doc 14 §9 (the eighth sidebar item absorbed by the existing three-group treatment unchanged — no grouping redesign). Chrome shown here is the SidebarLayout darkraise-ui variant (useLayoutStore); the TopNavLayout / StackedLayout alternates carry the same eight destinations and the same two scope controls, only the frame differs — that swap is chrome, not information architecture, so it is not re-illustrated here.

The project switcher and the context chip are two distinct controls, never one. The switcher (left, solid, a dot + project name) sets the project scope — the isolation boundary that rides into every query key (doc 13 §2). The chip (right, dashed-until-set) declares the optional session applies_when — the UI's equivalent of the X-Darkmem-Context header. Conflating them — e.g. letting a project named "production" silently imply env=prod — would silently exclude every dev-only fact from retrieval and surface an exclusion count the user never asked for: a quietly-lossy behaviour doc 13 §3 names explicitly. Rendered separately, each stays honest about what it does: switching project changes what data set is visible; setting or clearing the context chip changes which facts in that data set apply.
The chip's default state (not shown as the hero above) is unset — dashed border, no fill, label "no context declared". When unset, the backend falls back through its own precedence chain, down to the selected project's registry applies_when default at the lowest tier (doc 13 §3) — so a project still contributes a default, but only through that chain, never through the switcher masquerading as a context declaration.

Command palette (⌘K)

memo
Navigate
Jump to Memories ↵
Jump to Knowledge → Facts
Actions
Create memory… C
Switch project…
The palette is a global jump-and-act surface, not a third scope control — choosing a destination or action operates inside the current project/context scope; "Switch project…" opens the same switcher shown above rather than duplicating its logic. Results mix both groups (destinations, then actions) so the palette never becomes a second, competing navigation source.

C03 — switched-project variant: scope-refetch intent

Shown in one theme only (theme parity already demonstrated by the shared token system in the reference board above). Realises doc 13 §2's contract that the composite (project, status[, is_archived]) filter rides into the TanStack Query key, so switching the project switcher changes that key and every scoped view refetches against the new scope — never a client-side re-filter of an over-fetched set.
project: darkmem-core-backend → project: acme-storefront refetching
memories Memories list refetching
vaultFacts, vaultArticles, topics Knowledge tabs refetching
activityFeed, dreamDigest Activity refetching
overview, stats Dashboard calendar + tiles refetching
retrievalTrace why-retrieved trace (Memories) refetching
The context chip is untouched by this switch — it still reads "context: env=dev" exactly as before. That is the decoupling made visible: the switcher changed project and every key derived from it; nothing about the declared applies_when changed, because the two controls sit on independent axes (doc 13 §3). A design that tied them together would have to either clear the chip on every project switch (surprising) or carry a stale context into the new scope (also surprising) — keeping them separate avoids both failure modes.

C04 — Render-state skeleton

The reusable state pattern every screen instantiates on top of one .c04-surface shape: empty · loading · error · populated, plus the staged, degraded, and empty-with-exclusions variants (doc 13 §4, doc 14 §5). Each header chip below is one of the seven .state-chip variants already declared in mockup.css — this fragment is where they are first put on screen, composed rather than re-invented. populated renders as the hero in both themes; the other six render once, in the default theme, since the shared theme toggle guarantees parity.

Render state — empty

Honesty rule: empty says WHY. An empty result never renders as a bare blank — the copy states the cause and what happens next (doc 14 §5). The vault's cold-start register is reproduced verbatim below (doc 13 §5.1); the row underneath shows the other two registers doc 14 §5 names — no-match and healthy-empty — because one generic "nothing here" string cannot honestly cover all three.
Facts — project: darkmem empty
No corroborated facts yet no corroborated facts yet; candidates are served labelled in search Corroboration takes multiple distinct origins — this project has none logged yet.
no-match No matches in project darkmem for "cookie secure default" — clear filters or search all projects.
healthy-empty No disputes to adjudicate — the review queue is caught up.

Render state — loading

Loading is a layout preview, not a spinner replacing the page (doc 14 §5): skeleton rows mirror the exact chip / badge / text / meta slots the populated board below fills in, so the surface never jumps once data resolves.
Facts — project: darkmem loading

Render state — error

Honesty rule: error ≠ empty list. A both-sided channel failure raises a named error rather than returning zero rows indistinguishable from a genuine no-match (doc 07 §2, invariant 14) — retry stays offered and last-known cached data renders where cached, never silently swapped for an empty state. Honesty rule: partial names its failed step. A pipeline partial status never says just "something failed" — it names the failed phase (embed / extract / vector / graph, Phase 1–5) so the caller knows exactly what is missing.

S01 — Dashboard

The daily home screen (doc 13 §4): the contribution calendar (a GitHub-style UTC-day heatmap whose intensity ramp derives from --primary, doc 14 §6/§9), the live feed (the transient /ws stream), four stat tiles, and cold-start hints. The second stat tile counts the vault's corroborated rung by name — never labelled "verified" — per the global constraint on avoiding a status claim. Four states below: empty (fresh install), loading, error (retry + last-known counts), and populated (the hero, both themes).

Dashboard — empty (fresh install)

Honesty rule: empty is a fresh install, not a broken grid. The calendar still renders its full UTC-day grid — every cell honestly at level 0 — rather than collapsing to a blank panel; a first-capture call-to-action sits alongside it so a new install reads as "young," never "broken" (doc 13 §4: "the calendar is blank and a first-capture / onboarding call-to-action shows, not a broken grid").

Modules: stat tiles, the contribution calendar, and the live feed (doc 13 §4). The calendar's cells derive their fill from hsl(var(--primary) / alpha) composited over the theme's own card colour — the same alpha ramp reads pale-to-saturated in light mode and dark-to-luminous in dark mode purely from that compositing, satisfying the "mode-aware direction" requirement without a per-mode override (doc 14 §9: "a runtime lightness/alpha ramp off primary… direction mode-aware"). Every cell's title/aria-label prints its count, so intensity is never the sole carrier of the number (doc 14 §6). The second tile reads "Corroborated facts" — the vault's rung name, never "verified" — per the global constraint. The feed's third row shows a verification-transition event using the shared .badge rungs, reusing doc 14 §3's merge/person-check glyphs rather than inventing a new one.

S02 — Memories: populated (hero, both themes)

The two scope controls are distinct, never conflated (Global Constraints; doc 13 §3). The project scope pill mirrors the global project switcher — it sets project in every query key on this screen (invariant 14's isolation boundary). The context chip is a separate, optional control declaring the session applies_when (doc 07 §6) — it boosts/labels/ conflict-excludes rows, it does not scope which project's rows are visible. Conflating the two would silently exclude dev-only facts the moment someone switched to a project named "production."
The "supports fact F" nesting (doc 07 §5, doc 13 §4). A memory that is a source of a returned fact renders nested and indented under that fact, not as a third unrelated row — this is what "never triple-counted" means in practice. A disputed fact collapses to its badge plus a one-line both-sides summary in list context (doc 14 §3.5); the full split panel lives on the fact's own detail view (S07). An article's confidence is labelled claim-support coverage (doc 13 §5.2), never a vague score. Per-row "why retrieved" score breakdowns are S03's surface, not rendered here.

Score bars: chart-token identity, never the caution token. Every bar above resolves from only the four non-caution chart members — --chart-1 semantic, --chart-2 keyword, --chart-3 ppr (and its dual_level sibling at a lightness-shifted variant of the same token), --chart-5 rerank (and the rank_fusion_factor sub-arms at further lightness-shifted variants of that token) — --chart-4 is never used for an arm, so a bar can never be misread as a caution signal (doc 14 §4). Colour never carries the value alone: a number is printed beside every bar.
Dormant arms render dormant, never omitted, never zero. ppr is muted and labelled "inactive · ppr_enabled=false" on every row above — the channel did not run this request — and the same treatment applies to the importance/heat/ recency rank_fusion_factor sub-arms, whose weights are 0 in the envelope's weights snapshot. Omitting the bar would hide that the arm exists; drawing it at a literal zero would wrongly imply it ran and found nothing — this is invariant 23 read into the trace: built-but-unspent signals look built-but-unspent.
Grouping indents, never repeats as a sibling. The memory that supports the Facts-section fact nests directly under it with a dashed connector and its own full label cluster + score breakdown — it is still a fully-explained row, just visually subordinate to the fact it grounds (doc 14 §4).

Memory detail — deprecated

Also retained, not hidden. deprecated is the demoted end of the same lifecycle: when a memory that others point at via superseded_by is itself deleted (here, the TTL sweep in expired_memory_cleanup), its dependents are demoted to deprecated with superseded_by cleared to NULL first — the FK is ON DELETE SET NULL, so skipping that demotion would violate chk_superseded_has_pointer. That is why this board shows the amber .badge.deprecated with no successor link, unlike the superseded board above.

S06 — Knowledge · Facts tab: populated (hero, both themes)

Four filters, one project scope. subject free-texts over subject_name; relation constrains rel_type (the closed vocab); status constrains verification_status across all four rungs; project mirrors the global switcher and sets the isolation boundary the query key uses — a distinct control from the session context chip (Global Constraints), which this tab does not carry (context labels are per-fact applies_when data here, not a query input).
A candidate ranks below every verified rung, always (doc 08 §4, doc 14 §3.2). The list below sorts confirmed → corroborated → disputed → candidate; the candidate row at the bottom is "extracted signal, not yet corroborated" and is still served, labelled, never hidden and never mixed in as if equally supported. Each row composes the shared C01 badge markup verbatim — corroborated shows the filled claim inline, confirmed always renders visible text "human-ratified", and disputed collapses to a one-line both-sides summary (the full equal-weight split panel is S07's fact-detail surface). applies_when renders as one label per declared context key, or an explicit "no context restriction" label when the fact carries none — the module is never silently omitted.

S07 — Knowledge: Fact detail

/knowledge/facts/$factId — realising doc 13 §5.1 and doc 08 §3/§4: the fact text (subject_name / rel_type / object_name), the verification badge rendered verbatim, the sources module (fact_sources rows grouped by origin_key so the badge's count is auditable), the belief-window module (valid_at / invalid_at / expired_at as a timeline), and the applies_when context. Every module composes the shared vocabulary rather than re-deriving it: .badge / .layer-chip from mockup.css, and the dispute split panel + code@commit provenance list directly from C01-verification-badges.html. The corroborated base fact renders as the hero in both themes; the other four boards render once each in the default theme, since the shared toggle guarantees theme parity.

Fact detail — corroborated (hero, both themes)

The base case (doc 08 §4.1). K in the badge binds to COUNT(DISTINCT origin_key) over this fact's fact_sources rows, never a row count — the sources module below groups the raw rows by origin_key so that count is auditable rather than asserted. The belief-window module shows this fact's current, open window plus its prior, window-closed window on the same triple_key — the closed window is retained as history, not a live claim (doc 08 §3.1/§3.2, stale-on-arrival).

Fact detail — disputed, both-sides split panel

No picked winner (doc 08 §4.2, doc 14 §3.5). Both sides carry an overlapping validity window — that overlap is what makes this a genuine contradiction rather than a succession (disjoint windows would instead be modelled as two live facts, §3.1). Resolution happens only in the Review shell (doc 13 §6.2) — this page links there, it never adjudicates.

S09 — Article detail

One Layer-3 article — synthesised, grounded prose whose every claim links to the verified fact that entails it — realising doc 13 §5.2 and doc 09 §4. Every module composes the shared vocabulary rather than re-deriving it: the .badge rungs, the promoted .badge.superseded non-rung caution badge, and .overlay-stale, all from mockup.css; C04's skeleton classes for loading. Article detail — live, grounded (hero, both themes)

Grounding is enforced, not asserted (doc 09 §4.3). Every sentence in the Synthesised content module below carries an inline F# citation link — jump to the Citations module to see the exact fact it was checked against. The claim-support coverage readout is not a vague confidence score: it is the fraction of this article's candidate sentences a verified fact was found to entail, computed by the verification-purpose entailment pass over the synthesis draft, before anything ships.

Article

article: 4c9a7e21 subject: embedder-fingerprint-partitioning · concept project: darkmem synthesised: 2026-07-19 03:00 fact_set_hash: 8b31e9d2f4a7 applies_when: none — project-neutral
L3 · article corroborated asserted by 5 distinct origins of kinds [code, memory], no known contradiction, as of 2026-07-21

Claim-support coverage

confidence is labelled claim-support coverage, never a vague score — it is the entailed/total ratio over this article's candidate sentences (doc 09 §4.3, doc 04 §8.8).

0.86 claim-support coverage — 6 / 7 candidate sentences entailed by a cited fact
One drafted sentence — "the fingerprint slug embeds the embedding dimension so a dimension change always produces a new partition automatically" — failed the entailment check against its proposed citation (an unverified over-generalisation the synthesis model proposed) and was dropped before shipping. Every sentence rendered below is one of the 6 that passed; nothing uncited or unentailed is ever shown as knowledge. Had coverage fallen below the configured threshold, this article would not have shipped as corroborated at all — it would carry review_state=open and sit in the Review queue instead of rendering here (doc 09 §4.3); a disputed article is withheld the same way.

Synthesised content

grounded prose, organised by relation and applies_when context (doc 09 §4.2) — every sentence carries an inline citation to the fact that grounds it.

Partition boundary

Because pgvector requires a fixed-dimension vector(N) column, darkmem partitions embeddings by embedder fingerprint instead of storing every model's vectors in one table.F1 Each fingerprint gets its own four child tables — memory_embeddings__<slug>, entity_embeddings__<slug>, code_chunk_embeddings__<slug>, and entity_embedding_cache__<slug>.F2

Registration & safety

The embedders table is the fingerprint registry, and embedder_registry.register creates all four child tables idempotently with CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS.F3 Application code never names a partition directly; it always resolves the table name through child_table(parent, fingerprint).F4 _register_fingerprint must run before any insert into a partition — the ingest pipeline registers the content fingerprint in its embed phase, and re-registers mid-batch if the active embedder rotates.F5 A query that joins across two different fingerprints has no defined cosine distance, because vectors from different embedders are not comparable — cross-fingerprint joins are treated as a bug, not an edge case.F6

Citations — the article's only provenance

article_citations.fact_id is a hard FK to knowledge_triples — the one hard reference the design allows anywhere, safe because facts are invalidate-not-delete, never hard-deleted, so a citation can never dangle (doc 09 §4.3, doc 04 §8.8).

fact 7a3c1f02 claim_span [0,189) L2 · fact corroborated "pgvector requires a fixed-dimension vector(N) column, which is why darkmem partitions embeddings by embedder fingerprint"
fact 9d5e2b41 claim_span [190,361) L2 · fact corroborated "each embedder fingerprint gets four child tables — memory_embeddings, entity_embeddings, code_chunk_embeddings, entity_embedding_cache — each suffixed with the fingerprint slug"
fact c118e9af claim_span [365,520) L2 · fact corroborated "embedder_registry.register inserts the embedders row and creates the four child tables with CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, idempotently"
fact 2f6a04dd claim_span [524,640) L2 · fact corroborated "application code resolves a partition's table name through child_table(parent, fingerprint) and never names a partition directly"
fact e01b7c53 claim_span [644,812) L2 · fact corroborated "_register_fingerprint must be called before any insert into a partition; Phase 1 registers the content fingerprint, Phase 3 re-registers if the active embedder rotates mid-batch"
fact 88d4a6f1 claim_span [816,1010) L2 · fact corroborated "a query that joins across two different embedder fingerprints has no defined cosine distance"
The doc-16 firewall. This article's provenance is only the six cited facts listed above — it never reads a document block, and structurally it cannot: synthesis input is restricted to the subject's non-disputed corroborated/confirmed knowledge_triples rows (doc 09 §4.2), never a raw document. If a source document said something relevant, that content has to have already been extracted into its own verified fact before this article could ever cite it — there is no code path from a document straight into synthesised prose.

Scope of this fragment. Realises doc 09 §3.1/§3.4 and doc 13 §5/§9's Topics tab: the community list (memory_communities rows — label, dominant entities, impact rating, member count, report_string) and the pin-suggestion nominations that are the one bridge from topics to the article vault. Facts/Articles browsing are S06/S08's surfaces; the disputed/ungrounded review queue is S11's — this board composes only what doc 13 §5 assigns to Topics.
A topic is a community, never an entity (invariant 5, doc 01 §3.3, doc 09 §2). What this tab lists is a computed clustering of memories via their entities — it is never itself stored as an entity row, which would collide with the closed ENTITY_TYPES fallback and the entities table's UNIQUE(name, entity_type) constraint. Topics live in their own table (doc 06); this tab only ever renders them as a community.

S10 — Knowledge · Topics tab: populated (hero, both themes)

No verification badge on this tab (doc 09 §3.3). A community and a pin suggestion are organizational views of what memory contains — the same footing as memory_overview — never a verified claim, so neither card below composes .badge or .layer-chip; those belong to the Facts/Articles tabs (doc 13 §5.1/§5.2).
Community ids churn — nominations reference by label, never by id (doc 09 §3.4, doc 06 §7). memory_communities is delete-and-rewritten on every detection run, so a community id cached from a previous page load can point at nothing on the next. Every card below — and every events row an accept/dismiss journals — keys on the stable dominant-entity label ("Hybrid search & RRF weighting" below), never on the row's current id.
Accept pins a subject; it never auto-creates an article (doc 09 §3.4/§4.1). Accept writes a pinned subject only, making it eligible for synthesis on the next salience/synthesis pass — the article itself still has to be grounded from verified facts. Dismiss is recorded against the subject so later detection diffs suppress the suggestion, not merely hidden client-side. A nomination only fires once its subject already anchors a floor of non-disputed corroborated/confirmed facts — a human is never asked to pin a subject that could not yet be grounded.

S11 — Knowledge → Review mode (populated, hero)

Review mode is one of two modes of one shared shell. /knowledge/review is a single triage surface with a mode toggle — Review (this board) adjudicates truth, Hygiene (S12) curates housekeeping — not two routes; they read different backend review_state/status sets but are the same human activity, "triage a queue with actions" (doc 13 §6.2, doc 08 §6). Review mode renders review_state='open' rows: disputed facts shown with both conflicting sides, no picked winner, under-sourced facts held in demotion hysteresis, and ungrounded/low-confidence articles. The queue is consequence-ranked, never FIFO — retrieval frequency and subject salience order it, shown on each row rather than implied (doc 14 §6) — and every item stays served labelled in retrieval regardless of its queue state; review is a human override the queue holds open, never a gate the read path waits on (doc 08 §6). Both themes shown as the hero.

S11 — Ratify to human-ratified (AlertDialog, the strongest confirmation)

Ratify-to-confirmed is the single most consequential button in the product — the machine's ceiling is corroborated; only a human ratifying reaches confirmed, and that ratification writes a human-kind fact_source (who / when / what-was-shown), so a later re-extraction that withdraws every memory source still leaves this one and the fact survives (doc 08 §4.4). It therefore gets the language's strongest treatment: a solid accent button, the person-check glyph, and an AlertDialog restating the consequence before it commits (doc 14 §6). This action is authenticated REST/UI only — POST /api/v1/knowledge/facts/{id}/ratify (or /knowledge/articles/{id}/ratify) — and is never exposed over the unauthenticated MCP surface (doc 12 §3, doc 08 §4.4): no MCP tool can reach confirmed. Rendered once, default theme, since the shared toggle guarantees parity.
L2 · fact the reranker's default state in production
disputed 2 origins assert X, 1 origin asserts not-X
Ratify this fact? This records you as a human origin; the fact will render as human-ratified. The dispute above resolves in favour of the side you are ratifying — the other side's origins remain on record, they simply no longer block the rung. This cannot be undone by the machine; only another human action can reverse it. POST /api/v1/knowledge/facts/f-8821/ratify · authenticated · never exposed over the unauthenticated MCP surface

S12 — Knowledge: Hygiene mode, populated (hero, both themes)

Consequence-ranked, served-labelled, never a gate (doc 13 §6.2, doc 08 §6). Like Review, this queue is ranked by retrieval frequency and subject salience, never FIFO or insertion order — each row's muted why ranked here line makes that ranking visible instead of implied (doc 14 §6). Sitting in this queue changes nothing about how a row serves: a low-confidence memory keeps returning from search exactly as it does today, and a superseded chain keeps rendering its lineage link — hygiene is housekeeping the human works, never a bottleneck the read path waits on.
Four categories map onto the four named bulk actions (doc 08 §6, doc 08 §9). Candidate duplicates (associative-edge pairs dreaming flagged without a correction, doc 08 §9) get confirm dedup or, when one memory actually corrects the other rather than merely restating it, supersede instead — dreaming never hard-merges or deletes a memory itself. Low-confidence memories get set a TTL or prune; expiring-soon rows get extend the TTL or let expire — a row already on its way out is reprieved or allowed to lapse, never bulk-pruned outright. Superseded lineage gets prune to compact old chain links — pruning a memory another row still points superseded_by at first demotes that dependent to deprecated with the pointer cleared, so the chk_superseded_has_pointer constraint holds throughout the batch rather than aborting it.

Repositories — indexing (live phase ticker)

The live phase label is rewritten per tick, never a static "indexing…" spinner. Each repo.indexing_* broadcast over /ws advances this exact ticker (lib/websocket.ts, doc 13 §2.1); the fourteen phases are doc 10 §2's fixed pipeline topology, unchanged by the reshape. enrich_symbols and generate_wiki were left off for this run, so phases 13–14 are labelled skipped — opt-in, not requested rather than silently missing from the list.

Repositories — stale (fail-stale banner, T1)

Honesty rule: fail-stale, not fail-empty. A pipeline exception no longer wipes the repo graph (the old behaviour was _delete_all_repo_data on any exception, which could wipe-and-error loop). The last-good graph stays in place, labelled stale, and every code tool (code_search, code_symbol, code_context, …) keeps serving it — degraded honesty, never an emptied graph (doc 10 §3, invariant 14).
payments-service stale last-good HEAD 4b7e120
Last index failed — serving the last-good graph, marked stale Cause: an unhandled exception during phase 09 (community detection) — the Leiden partitioning step timed out. The run failed before reaching phase 14, and nothing was deleted. The graph indexed 2026-07-19 14:02 UTC (HEAD 4b7e120) is still served to every code tool, labelled stale, until the next run succeeds.
auto_sync will also retry on the next scheduled sync — the stale label clears automatically the moment a run succeeds.

Repositories — error (clone/index failure)

Honesty rule: the failure message is surfaced, not summarised away. Repeated auto_sync failures disable sync and record the raw cause in pipeline_failures (per-repo, doc 10 §3); this is distinct from the stale case above — here indexing never completed even once for the current HEAD attempt, so there is no fresher graph being withheld, only a named blocker and a manual way past it.
internal-tools-cli error auto_sync disabled
Clone failed — 3 consecutive attempts auto_sync disabled after the third failure to protect the sync loop from spinning on a broken remote. git@github.com:acme/internal-tools-cli.git — Permission denied (publickey). Could not read from remote repository.

Reindex dialog — the three toggles

POST /repos/{id}/reindex accepts exactly {full, enrich_symbols, generate_wiki}, all default false (doc 10 §8). Structural indexing (the symbol/edge graph, communities, processes, chunk embeddings) always runs regardless of these toggles — they only gate the two LLM-cost-heavy phases (13, 14) and whether the diff is discarded in favour of a full rebuild.

full Rebuild the entire repo graph from scratch, ignoring last_indexed_commit. Off runs the incremental diff (changed files only since the last indexed HEAD).
enrich_symbols Drain the pending-symbol LLM-summary backlog inline during this run, bounded and scoped to this repo. Off leaves symbols draining lazily via the code_enrichment background job.
generate_wiki Generate the LLM wiki over the graph after this run completes. GET /code/wiki is read-only and never triggers generation on its own — this toggle is the only way a wiki gets built.

Overview

backend/app is a FastAPI service organised into api/routes (REST), api/mcp (the FastMCP tool family mounted at /mcp), services (the ingestion pipeline and its supporting orchestration), repositories (graph, relational, and vector data access), and models/schemas. The process entry point is app/main.py, which also registers the seven periodic jobs under JobRegistry.

Ingestion pipeline

ProcessingPipeline.process_batch is the central write path. It moves a batch of memories through five phases — content embed, extract-and-classify, entity embed with cache, dedup, and write — committing the vector and graph halves of phase five in separate savepoints so a graph failure never rolls back the vector write.

  • services/pipeline.py — phase orchestration, savepoint boundaries
  • services/extraction_clean.py — entity/relationship extraction
  • services/code_pipeline.py — this repository's own indexing path

S18 — Activity: five-phase pipeline stepper

The per-memory module of the Activity shell (doc 13 §6.1, doc 02 §5.2): each captured memory's progress through content embed → extract-and-classify → entity embed → dedup → write, ending in one of three honest terminal states — completed, partial, or failed. A partial memory always names exactly which step broke, using pipeline_failures.failed_step's durable named-step vocabulary as derive_memory_failed_step resolves it — content_embedding, extraction, extraction_partial, vector_write, graph_write — never a collapsed batch pass/fail (invariant 14). The /ws payload (PipelineStatus) carries a different, shorter set of fields for the same four checkpoints — embed / extract / vector / graph, each resolving to ok / error / partial / skipped — which derive_memory_failed_step reads to produce the named step above; the two vocabularies are related, not identical. Entity embed and dedup (phases 3–4) are batch-level ANN operations that degrade gracefully on a miss rather than failing a single memory, so the named-failure vocabulary only ever points at phase 1 (content_embedding), phase 2 (extraction / extraction_partial), or one of phase 5's two savepoints (vector_write / graph_write).

S18 — pipeline stepper: running

The non-terminal state every memory starts in once claimed from the buffer (doc 02 §5.2: [*] → running : claimed from buffer). The pipeline broadcasts exactly one terminal pipeline.* event per memory, after all five phases finish (pipeline.py, the process_memory broadcast) — PipelineStatus (events.py) has no progress or current-phase field, and there is no pipeline.running / pipeline.progress event, so the client has no way to know which phase is currently executing. The stepper below renders every node pending — it is the decomposition the one eventual terminal broadcast resolves into, not a live per-phase progress bar.

S18 — pipeline stepper: failed

Terminal — failed. pipeline.failed fires only when every checkpoint that actually ran reports non-ok — a single early failure whose later steps still land as skipped (not attempted) is not enough on its own; here content embedding and extraction both errored independently, so vector and graph write never ran. derive_memory_failed_step checks hard errors in phase order and the first one wins, so the named step is content_embedding even though extraction failed too.

S19 — Activity: live feed

The Activity screen's live view (doc 13 §2.1/§6.1): the transient /ws stream while this view stays open, rendered as an ordered feed list, plus the dispute-toast still-frame — the one transient toast that carries honesty content, a fact.verified dispute alert (doc 13 §2.1, spec §6). The toast's motion (slide-in, auto-dismiss timer) is explicitly out of scope for this deliverable; only the frozen frame is authored. Four states below for the feed itself: empty, loading, error, populated (hero, both themes); the still-frame is a fifth, dedicated board.

Activity — live feed — empty

Honesty rule: empty says why, scoped to what a transient stream can honestly claim. This is not the vault's cold-start register (doc 13 §5.1) — the project may have years of history. The feed only ever shows what has streamed over /ws since this view mounted, so its empty copy says exactly that: nothing has arrived in this open session, not "no activity ever" (doc 14 §5's three registers, applied to a fourth, session-scoped case this screen introduces).
Activity — live feed /activity empty
No live events since this view opened The feed streams only while Activity stays open — captures, pipeline runs, repo syncs, and verification changes will appear here the moment they happen. For history before this view was opened, see the per-object timeline or the calendar day drill-down, which read the durable events substrate rather than this transient stream (doc 13 §2.1/§6.4).

Activity — live feed — loading

Loading is the initial /ws handshake, not a spinner replacing the page (doc 14 §5): skeleton rows mirror the exact chip / badge / text / time slots the populated board below fills in, so the surface never jumps once the socket connects and the first events arrive.

Honesty rule: error ≠ empty list, and a lost socket is never the only record. When reconnection is exhausted, the panel raises a named disconnect with a manual retry rather than quietly reverting to an empty list — and the last-known events stay visible, dimmed, because a WebSocket message lost on disconnect must never be the sole record of what happened (doc 13 §2.1: "a WebSocket message is lost on a disconnect, so it may never be the *only* record of a lifecycle transition"). The durable events substrate backs the timeline and calendar regardless of this socket's state.

The one transient toast that carries honesty content, frozen. Per the WebSocket-to-invalidation mapping (doc 13 §2.1), several events fire a toast (a finished retry batch, a terminal repo state, a finished dream cycle) but those are operational notices; the fact.verified dispute is the only one whose toast body itself states an epistemic claim, so it is the one rendered here. The toast collapses to the badge plus a one-line both-sides summary — the same collapse rule the split-panel detail view uses in list contexts (doc 14 §3.5) — so a fast-moving alert can never say something the detail view (S07/C01) later contradicts. S20 — Activity · Failure triage

The v1 failure triage module of the Activity shell (doc 13 §6.1): pipeline_failures rows — the same table derive_memory_failed_step and the code pipeline's derive_code_failed_step write into today — each naming its failed step and its reason, with a per-row retry (POST /api/v1/pipeline-failures/{id}/retry) and a header-level retry all (POST /api/v1/pipeline-failures/retry-all). A row whose attempts counter keeps climbing on the same failed step is surfaced as poison rather than left to retry unnoticed — the visual counterpart to the buffer-monitor's "attempts exceeded" poison state doc 13 §6.1 describes for the staged memory_buffer, applied here to the triage surface that already ships.

Failure triage — empty (healthy)

Healthy-empty, not "nothing here." Zero unresolved rows in pipeline_failures is a positive state, not an absence to explain away (doc 14 §5's third empty register: "a queue at zero"), so the copy states plainly that recent runs completed cleanly rather than rendering a bare blank indistinguishable from a broken triage list.

A failed GET /api/v1/pipeline-failures request is not the same thing as "no failures" — conflating the two would hide real unresolved rows behind a healthy-looking empty state. The named failure keeps the last-known unresolved count visible and offers retry, matching the language's standard error treatment (doc 14 §5).

S21 — Activity · job board

The job-board module of Activity (doc 13 §6.1, doc 02 §5.3): the seven JobRegistry jobs with their cron schedule, last-run/next-run, and status; the per-job config gear dialog (cron expression, the min_interval_seconds floor, the max_run_seconds ceiling, and any config_schema fields); the manual trigger action; and the busy (HTTP 409) outcome when a trigger lands on a lock the scheduled loop already holds — it is never queued behind the running job. Each job's cron may be five-field (minute precision) or six-field (seconds-first, Quartz-style); next-run is computed from that expression via croniter.

Job board — empty (fresh install, no run history yet)

Honesty rule: empty says why, and here it cannot mean "no jobs." All seven jobs are registered in code at process startup (app/main.py) — the list itself can never legitimately render zero rows. The honest empty condition for this screen is a fresh install with no run history: every job exists and is scheduled, but none has fired yet, so last-run is never and next-run is the job's first computed tick. Rendering a fabricated "no jobs configured" state instead would misstate what this backend can produce (doc 14 §5's why-honesty rule, applied to a list that structurally cannot be absent).

Per-job config gear dialog — cron (edited elsewhere) / floor & ceiling (read-only) / config_schema (editable)

Opened from the gear on code_enrichment above. min_interval_seconds (the floor: the loop will not fire more often than this regardless of what the cron expression computes) and max_run_seconds (the ceiling on a single run's duration) are fixed Job-dataclass attributes set once at registration in app/main.py — there is no write path for either, so both render read-only here, the same treatment as cron above them. The only field this dialog can actually save lives below, under this job's own config_schema (a FieldDescriptor list declared at registration) — for code_enrichment that's a single field, batch_size. cron and enabled are edited through a separate endpoint, PUT /api/v1/jobs/{key}; config_schema fields go through PUT /api/v1/jobs/{key}/config, which validates every field against its declared type and min/max, rejects unknown keys, and writes under the same per-job lock the scheduled tick and manual trigger already share — a save can never race a running tick.
Configure — code_enrichment config row: job:code_enrichment
cronschedule · read-only here
Six-field, seconds-first (Quartz-style): every 10 seconds. Five-field expressions (minute precision) are also accepted. Edited via PUT /api/v1/jobs/{key}, not this dialog's Save.
min_interval_secondsfloor · read-only
The loop will not fire more often than this floor, no matter how aggressive the cron above computes. A Job-dataclass constant fixed at registration — not editable via config.
max_run_secondsceiling · read-only
A run still executing past this ceiling is treated as overrun. Also a registration-time constant, not editable via config.
config_schema — job-specific, editable field
batch_sizeint
Code symbols summarised per scheduled run. min 1 · max 100
config_schema writes acquire the same lock the scheduled tick uses.

Manual trigger on a held lock — busy (HTTP 409), never queued

Honesty rule: busy is a protection, not a failure, and it is not a queue. trigger(key) acquires the same per-job asyncio.Lock the scheduled loop holds while a tick is running, so a manual run and a scheduled run can never race. A trigger that lands while the lock is held returns busy → HTTP 409 immediately — the request is discarded, never queued behind the in-flight run, and the human must retry once it finishes rather than stacking a second execution (doc 02 §5.3).

S22 — Activity · Staged monitors

Doc 13 §6.1 stages two of Activity's six modules behind backends that do not exist yet: the buffer-depth monitor (needs memory_buffer, doc 04 §8.6) and the dream-run monitor (needs the consolidation job family, doc 08 §5). The other four — the five-phase stepper (S18), the live feed (S19), failure triage (S20), and the job board (S21) — already ship. Invariant 23 governs how a staged module is allowed to render: a live-looking panel bound to a table that never writes would read as either broken or as a shipped-capability claim, so it stays labelled staged until its signal exists — never a bare empty panel. To let this design still be reviewed in full, each module below appears twice: once as the honestly labelled staged placeholder that ships today's Activity, and once as its fully populated target design, so the whole target surface is visible without any board claiming it ships.

Buffer-depth monitor — staged

Why staged, not empty (invariant 23). memory_buffer does not exist yet — Tier-A capture still acks straight into the five-phase pipeline with no durable queue in front of it, so there is no pending/claimed/done/error data this panel could honestly show. A live-looking gauge here would either read as broken or imply the durable buffer already ships; the phase-labelled placeholder is the honest alternative doc 14 §5's staged pattern defines.

Buffer-depth monitor — populated target design (hero, both themes)

The full target surface, not a live claim (invariant 23). This is what the buffer-depth monitor renders once memory_buffer ships, visualised in full so the design can be signed off without this board implying the backend exists today — the staged board above is what actually ships until then.
The memory_buffer state machine (doc 04 §8.6). A captured memory lands pending the instant Tier A acks (202), before the five-phase pipeline claims it. A buffer_flush worker claims a batch with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (fixing memobase's double-flush bug), flips it to claimed, then done once flushed — done rows are swept past a short retention window so the table never grows unbounded. A row whose attempts counter exceeds the retry threshold flips to error instead of retrying forever: a poison row, surfaced here and in Failure triage (S20) rather than silently looping.

S23 — Activity: Dream digest, populated (hero, both themes)

Grouped, reversible ledger entries (doc 14 §6, doc 08 §7). Each row carries its action-type chip, its object link, a compact before→after rendering for status/pointer changes, and its undo affordance. The register is deliberately calm — neutral chips for routine dream actions; the caution role (amber) appears only on a row that touched a disputed object or demoted a rung, never on the group as a whole, since one group can mix routine and caution-worthy entries. Undo is a standard outline button, not destructive-red — every inverse is a journaled restore, not a deletion — and undo is an authenticated curation action (doc 08 §7, doc 12), same auth boundary as ratify.
Seven action types, five summary tiles. The grouped list realises all seven action types doc 13 §6.3 names: supersession, refine, associative-edge derivation, fact promotion/demotion, ratification, fact invalidation, article re-synthesis. The cycle-summary strip above them matches doc 13 §6.3's five named counts exactly (superseded / refined / promoted–demoted / disputed / edges derived) — ratification is counted within the promoted figure (a human ratifying is a promotion to confirmed) but still gets its own group below, since its inverse differs: withdrawing a human-kind fact_source, not restoring a prior verification_status. Invalidation and re-synthesis are rarer this cycle (one each) and don't earn a dedicated summary tile, but every action type still gets its own grouped section and undo, per doc 08 §7's table of seven reversible actions.
Honesty rule: an action past its undo window is disabled, with the reason printed inline — never hidden, never a broken button (doc 14 §6, doc 08 §7). Two distinct causes disable undo: a newer change rewrote the same object after this cycle acted on it (the before-state undo would restore is no longer current), or dream_undo_retention elapsed since the action. Both are shown below — one inline in the Supersession group, two more in the collapsed "earlier cycles" section, since retention (illustrated here as 7 days, a config row) rarely elapses within the latest cycle's own few-minute window.

S23 — Undo a batch (AlertDialog, since it spans many objects)

Per-batch undo confirms through AlertDialog; per-action undo does not (doc 14 §6). A single action's undo is a low-consequence, fully-reversible restore of one object, so the outline button commits directly. A batch spans many objects at once, so it gets the stronger confirmation treatment — listing exactly what will be restored — before it commits. Undo remains a standard outline/primary treatment, not destructive-red: every inverse here is a journaled restore, never a deletion (doc 08 §7). Rendered once, default theme, since the shared toggle guarantees parity.

S24 — Activity: calendar day drill-down

/activity/day/$date — a calendar-day click drills into that UTC day-bucket's slice of the durable events substrate (doc 13 §6.4, doc 04 §8.1). This is the same event-row component the per-object timeline renders (doc 14 §6, realised for one memory in S05): timestamp, an event-type chip (neutral role, drawn from the closed event_type vocabulary), an object link, and — only for verification transitions — the from→to rung pair as two small .badge pills joined by an arrow. Every module composes the shared vocabulary: .badge rungs from mockup.css, and C04's surface/skeleton/alert/empty classes for the non-populated states. populated renders as the hero in both themes; loading, error, and empty render once each in the default theme, since the shared toggle guarantees theme parity.

The feature-flags/tunables tab of the flattened Settings IA (doc 13 §7): the seven rank_fusion_factor / RRF-list / context-boost w_* ranking-arm weights (doc 04 §9, doc 07 §3/§6/§11), the three graph-augmentation *_enabled flags (doc 07 §4/§11), the corroboration N promotion gate with its diversity/time rule (doc 08 §4.1), and a job-cadence summary (doc 02 §5.3). Every value here is a config row read through get_feature_flags_dict's merge-over-coded-defaults (5-second TTL single-flight cache) — nothing on this screen is computed, only read and written.

S26 — Settings · LLM

The flattened LLM configuration surface (doc 13 §7, doc 11, doc 04 §7): six inline purpose cards — embedding / extraction / classification / reasoning / summarization / reranker — each editing {model, base_url, api_key, api_kind, params, dimensions?, reasoning?} directly on the row, no indirection. The classification card carries the inline classifier_kind toggle (llm | local); the summarization card carries the three code-summarization buckets (symbol / module / overview). There is deliberately no provider/profile/ml-profile chrome — those management surfaces are removed with the flattening, shown struck through below rather than omitted silently. api_kind renders as a plain selector; every vendor auth/reasoning/structured-output quirk it selects resolves server-side (doc 11 §4) and is never re-implemented here. A save triggers the live-reload confirmation, because there are no LLM_* env vars and the change takes effect without a redeploy (invariants 18/19).

Settings · LLM — empty

Honesty rule: empty says why, and here it cannot mean "no purposes configured." All six purpose rows are written by the setup wizard's finalize step (app/services/llm_seed.py, doc 11 §7) before any authenticated route — Settings included — becomes reachable, and every seed defaults to the local Ollama install so a no-credentials fresh install still ends up with six live rows. So this grid cannot legitimately show zero cards for a running install. The one honest empty condition left is a config-integrity gap: the llm_purpose_configs table was reset (a DB restore, a re-run migration) without re-running the wizard's finalize step, so the six-row read genuinely comes back empty. The empty state names that condition and offers the one recovery action that actually fixes it, rather than inventing a picker over rows that do not exist.
No purpose rows found llm_purpose_configs read zero rows — the setup wizard's finalize step has not seeded this install (or the table was reset after it ran) This is not a "no purposes exist by design" state — every install needs all six rows to serve embedding, extraction, and chat calls at all.

No provider/profile chrome renders here, at any state — not even a disabled picker. darkmem is not an LLM proxy: each purpose is one row the operator edits directly, so the llm_providers / llm_profiles / ml_profiles tables and every *_ref column are dropped outright with this flattening (doc 04 §7, doc 11 §2). A profile picker over a schema with no profiles table would be scaffolding rendered as a feature (invariant 23, doc 13 §7) — so the honest move is deletion, not a greyed-out control that implies a capability this schema no longer has anywhere to store.

Save → live-reload confirmation

No LLM_* env vars exist — a save takes effect without a redeploy (invariants 18/19). On save the app constructs a fresh LLMOrchestrator from the current six purpose rows and swaps the in-process reference atomically; there is no second worker to notify and no shared external cache to invalidate (doc 11 §3, invariant 13 — single uvicorn worker is what makes the swap atomic without cross-worker coordination). The superseded client's connection pool drains rather than dropping in-flight calls.
Saved — reasoning purpose updated The orchestrator was rebuilt from all six purpose rows and the live reference was swapped in-process. This change is already serving requests — no redeploy needed.

orchestratornew instance built from six purpose rows, reference swapped atomically
superseded clientdraining — closes once in-flight calls finish
redeploy neededno — config lives in DB rows, read at boot and on live reload

S27 — Settings · Jobs

The JobRegistry configuration surface (doc 13 §7, doc 02 §5.3) for the same seven registered jobs S21's Activity job board monitors — read here for editing rather than operating. This screen edits cron and enabled per job (PUT /api/v1/jobs/{key}) and any job-declared config_schema fields (PUT /api/v1/jobs/{key}/config); min_interval_seconds (the floor) and max_run_seconds (the ceiling) stay read-only registration constants here, exactly as they do on S21's gear dialog — there is no write path for either. Both writes share the job's asyncio.Lock with the scheduled loop, so a save can never race a running tick; a cron-only edit takes effect on the job's next scheduled tick, while flipping enabled restarts the loop immediately. Run history, the manual Trigger now action, and the busy (HTTP 409) outcome live on S21's Activity job board, not here.

Honesty rule: empty says why, and here it cannot mean "no jobs." All seven jobs are registered in code at process startup (app/main.py) — the list itself can never legitimately render zero rows, same invariant as S21's empty board. The honest empty condition for a configuration surface is different from S21's "no run history": no config row exists yet for any job, so every field below is load_config's synthesized default (the job's default_cron, an implicit enabled switch, and each declared config_schema field's own default) rather than a persisted override — nothing is written until the first Save.

S28 — Settings · Security

The Security tab (doc 13 §7, doc 18): auth (the admin password-change form and the signed-in session's cookie-JWT state), tokens (the refresh/blocklist rotation state and the mass-revocation-by-iat rule a password change triggers), and TOFU status (the trust-on-first-use setup claim and the require_uninitialized gate it leaves behind). The panel also renders the LAN trust model honestly as the v1 committed posture (doc 18 §2: /mcp unauthenticated behind the Host allowlist only, /api/v1+/ws behind the human cookie, /setup as TOFU) and keeps the dormant ApiKey bearer path visibly Phase‑4, designed but not wired — every write today still passes api_key_id=None — so nothing on this screen ever overclaims a credential path that does not exist yet (invariant 23).

Security — empty (fresh install, just past the TOFU claim)

Honesty rule: empty says why, and here it cannot mean "no security config." Auth and TOFU status are never legitimately absent — the moment the setup wizard finalizes, admin_password_hash exists and require_uninitialized is already gating /setup. The honest empty condition for this screen is a fresh box with zero event history: no token rotations yet, no lockouts yet, the MCP allowlist still at its shipped default (localhost-only, MCP_ALLOWED_HOSTS unset). The TOFU status card below is this board's required verification surface (doc 13 §7) and it already reads claimed, never "empty" — a bootstrap outcome is not a list that can have zero rows.

darkmem trusts its LAN, authenticates its human, and attributes — but does not authenticate — its agents (doc 18 §1). Three postures, one service layer underneath all of them:
/mcpHost allowlist only, no credential

The one authenticated door on this box; /ws rejects a missing/invalid/revoked token with close code 1008 before joining the broadcast set.

See the Setup card above — closes itself permanently the moment the first wizard run completes.

S29 — Settings · Maintenance

The Maintenance tab of Settings (doc 13 §7): three operator-facing modules — re-embed (backfilling memories/entities/code chunks missing a vector under the currently active embedder fingerprint, doc 04 §5), cleanup ops (one-click triggers for the orphan-entity, orphan-tag, and expired-memory JobRegistry jobs, plus a count-and-link-out to unresolved pipeline failures), and DB ops (per-fingerprint cache pruning and the Postgres-level housekeeping a heavy re-embed or cleanup pass leaves behind). Every trigger opens an inline confirmation before it runs — re-embed's confirms cost and duration (it only backfills missing rows, it deletes nothing), cleanup's and DB ops' confirm data loss.

Maintenance — empty (nothing currently needs attention)

Honesty rule: empty here cannot mean "modules unavailable." All three modules always exist — the empty condition is a healthy quiescent vault: every memory/entity has a row under the active fingerprint, zero unresolved pipeline_failures, and no cache to prune. Same discipline S21's job board applies to "no run history yet" (this board's sibling for the shared cleanup jobs): the honest empty state names what is actually absent, never fabricates "no maintenance available."
Re-embed empty
Active fingerprint bge-large-en-v1.5|1024 — 0 memories, 0 entities, 0 code chunks missing a vector. Nothing to backfill.
Cleanup ops empty
0 orphan entities, 0 orphan tags, 0 expired memories, 0 unresolved pipeline failures. All three cleanup jobs are still scheduled (doc 02 §5.3) — there is simply nothing pending right now.
DB ops empty
No retired embedder caches to prune (this is the only embedder darkmem has ever used). No maintenance run logged yet.

Maintenance — loading

Skeleton bars mirror each card's header + first two rows so the board does not reflow once GET /api/v1/reembed/obsolete-counts and GET /api/v1/pipeline-failures/counts resolve (doc 14 §5).
loading
loading
loading

Maintenance — error

Honesty rule: error ≠ empty grid. When GET /api/v1/reembed/obsolete-counts itself fails (a database or transport error), the board raises a named error rather than a card indistinguishable from the honest empty state above (invariant 14). This is deliberately not the "no active embedder" case: get_obsolete_counts does not guard with _resolve_fingerprint, so an uninitialized pipeline returns 200 with every count quietly zeroed instead — the exact zeroed-vs-empty risk this honesty rule exists to catch. Cleanup ops and DB ops do not depend on this read and stay usable; only the re-embed card is blocked.
Couldn't load re-embed status GET /api/v1/reembed/obsolete-counts request failed (database/transport error). Note this is distinct from a missing embedder: with no active embedder, that endpoint does not 503 — it returns 200 with {memories: 0, entities: 0, code_chunks: 0, current_fingerprint: ""}. The routes that genuinely 503 on a missing embedder are the drill-down list endpoints (list_obsolete_*) and prune-cache, via _resolve_fingerprint. Cleanup ops and DB ops below are unaffected. Retry

Maintenance — populated (hero, both themes)

Every trigger below opens the same inline armed-confirmation shape before it runs (never a bare destructive click): re-embed's confirm names cost and duration only — the backfill upserts missing rows under the active fingerprint, it never deletes an existing vector, so its panel stays on the caution (--warning) token. The expired-memory sweep and the cache prune actually delete/drop rows, so their panels escalate to the conflict (--destructive) token — the same colour-by-consequence split doc 14 §3.1 uses for badges, reused here for a different kind of honesty signal (what happens if you click Confirm). VACUUM ANALYZE / REINDEX carry the illustrative tag: standard Postgres housekeeping surfaced here because it is where an operator would reach for it after a heavy re-embed or cleanup pass, not because a dedicated darkmem endpoint exists for either yet (only the cache prune and the three cleanup jobs are real routes today) — flagged rather than silently implied as shipped.

Re-embed 182 memories now? Dispatches 182 embedding calls to the live embedding-purpose LLM. Not destructive — existing vectors under other fingerprints are left alone — but it cannot be cancelled once started, only blocked from a second concurrent run on this category (409 already_running).

Re-embed 47 entities now? Dispatches 47 embedding calls to the live embedding-purpose LLM. Not destructive — existing vectors under other fingerprints are left alone — but it cannot be cancelled once started, only blocked from a second concurrent run on this category (409 already_running).

expired_memory_cleanup14 past expires_at
